cse-2011-cs-45.approach: Read off the language of $D$, then minimise it by partition refinement: merge equivalent states and keep the ones a suffix can tell apart. Compare the result with each option, rejecting wrong ones with a single counter-example string.

steps.title: Language of D
steps.body:
From $p$: reading `a` reaches accepting $s$, which loops on everything. Reading `b` reaches $q$; from $q$, `a` reaches accepting $t$ (loops on everything) and `b` reaches the dead state $r$.

$$L(D)=a(a+b)^*\;+\;ba(a+b)^*$$

so $L(D)$ is the set of strings that start with `a` or with `ba`.

scene.caption: D: start p, accepting s and t

steps.title: Merge equivalent states
steps.body:
Start with the partition $\{s,t\}$ (accepting) and $\{p,q,r\}$ (non-accepting).

- $s$ and $t$ both accept every suffix, and on both symbols they stay in $\{s,t\}$, so $s\equiv t$.
- $r$ rejects every suffix and is a dead state.
- $p$ and $q$: on `b`, $p\to q$ but $q\to r$. The suffix `ba` is accepted from $p$ (`ba` takes it to $t$) and rejected from $q$ (`ba` takes it to $r$). So $p\not\equiv q$.
- $p,q$ vs $r$: suffix `a` is accepted from $p$ and $q$ but not from $r$.

The classes are $\{p\},\{q\},\{r\},\{s,t\}$, so the minimal DFA has **4 states**.

scene.caption: s ≡ t (both accept everything); p, q, r are pairwise distinguishable

steps.title: Build the minimal DFA
steps.body: Replace $t$ by $s$: $p\xrightarrow{a}s$, $p\xrightarrow{b}q$, $q\xrightarrow{a}s$, $q\xrightarrow{b}r$, with $r$ looping on $a,b$ and accepting $s$ looping on $a,b$. This is exactly option **(A)**.

answer.value: Option (A): the 4-state DFA with t merged into s

optionAnalysis.reason: It is $D$ with the equivalent states $s,t$ merged. It accepts exactly the strings that start with `a` or `ba`, and it has 4 states, which is the minimum.
The string `b` takes $p$ to accepting $q$, so `b` is accepted, but $D$ rejects `b`.
`b` is accepted (it ends in accepting $q$), which is wrong. It is not even a DFA, because $q$ has two `b` transitions (to $q$ and to $r$).
`bba` is accepted ($p\to q\to q\to s$), but $D$ rejects it ($p\to q\to r$). There is no dead state for strings that start with `bb`.

cse-2011-cs-45.shortcut: Describe the language as "starts with a or ba". Then test each option on `b` and `bba`. Only (A) rejects both and accepts `a` and `ba`.
pitfalls: Merging $p$ and $q$ because both go to an accepting state on `a`. The suffix `ba` tells them apart.
Forgetting that a complete DFA needs the dead state $r$.
cse-2011-cs-45.verification: Tested `a`, `ba`, `b`, `bb`, `bba` and `aab` on $D$ and on (A). The two machines agree on all of them.
